title: Can a big common factor make the rows of division shorter?
description: Two pairs, ninety and one hundred fifty, and eighty four and one hundred thirty two, are divided by a big common factor first. The divisors give the highest common factor, and the divisors with the last row give the lowest common multiple. Keeko doubts this and stops too early, saying nine and fifteen share nothing.
teaching_notes: One idea: divide by any common factor you can see, and stop only when the last row shares no prime. Watch for students who stop at a row such as nine and fifteen, which still share three.

source: Use bigger common divisors to find the HCF and LCM of 90 and 150, and of 84 and 132.
video_script.why: The child has divided by one prime at a time and now sees that any common factor can be used, which shortens the rows.
video_script.substitution: Divide both numbers by a big common factor, again and again, until the last row shares no prime.
video_script.anchor: Rows of division for ninety and one hundred fifty, and for eighty four and one hundred thirty two, in the way the two children of the book write them.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko stops after dividing by ten, but nine and fifteen still share the prime three.
video_script.payoff_line: Ninety and one hundred fifty have highest common factor thirty and lowest common multiple four hundred fifty

final_answer.spoken: for ninety and one hundred fifty, thirty and four hundred fifty; for eighty four and one hundred thirty two, twelve and nine hundred twenty four

names.Jia: divides by a big common factor first, to find the HCF and LCM
names.Ruhee: also removes the bigger common factors first

video_script.design: One idea: any common factor can be a divisor, and the last row must share no prime. The rows for both pairs stay on the board.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Jia and Ruhee found a faster way. They divide by a big common factor first, not only by a prime.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Use this way on ninety and one hundred fifty. Then use it on eighty four and one hundred thirty two.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Which number bigger than a prime goes into both ninety and one hundred fifty?

beats.on_screen: the two pairs stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a row of division with a big divisor on the left; the words highest common factor and lowest common multiple appear one by one

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Both numbers can be divided by any common factor we can see, not only by a prime.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The largest number that divides both numbers is called the highest common factor.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The smallest number that is a multiple of both is called the lowest common multiple.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The divisors on the left give the first. The divisors with the last row give the second.

marks.m1: the given line is written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, the pairs ninety and one hundred fifty, and eighty four and one hundred thirty two.

beats.on_screen: To find: the HCF and the LCM of each pair

marks.m1: the find line is written under the given line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find the highest common factor and the lowest common multiple of each pair.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: 10 | 90, 150 gives 9, 15. 3 | 9, 15 gives 3, 5. No common prime, so stop

marks.m1: the divisor 10 and the row 9, 15 are written
marks.m2: the prime 3 is shown inside both 9 and 15
marks.m3: the divisor 3, the last row 3, 5 and a stop sign are written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, take ninety and one hundred fifty. Both end in zero, so divide both by ten to get nine and fifteen.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>These still share the prime three.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Divide both by three to get three and five. These share no prime, so we stop.

marks.m1: the divisors 10 and 3 are joined by a multiplication sign
marks.m2: the last row 3, 5 is added to the product for the LCM

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, the highest common factor multiplies the divisors, ten and three.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The lowest common multiple multiplies the divisors and the last row, ten, three, three and five.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: 12 | 84, 132 gives 7, 11. No common prime, so stop

marks.m1: the divisor 12 and the last row 7, 11 are written
marks.m2: a stop sign appears beside the last row

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, take eighty four and one hundred thirty two. Twelve goes into both, so divide both by twelve to get seven and eleven.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>These share no prime, so we stop.

marks.m2: the last row 7, 11 is added to the divisor in a product

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, here there is only one divisor, twelve, so it makes the highest common factor.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The lowest common multiple multiplies twelve, seven and eleven.

marks.m1: the answers for the first pair are written and boxed
marks.m2: the answers for the second pair are written and boxed
marks.m3: the check lines are written below

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Ninety and one hundred fifty have highest common factor thirty and lowest common multiple four hundred fifty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>For eighty four and one hundred thirty two, they are twelve and nine hundred twenty four.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Thirty goes into ninety three times, and into one hundred fifty five times.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the row 9, 15
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: the row 9, 15 with the word stop; 9 = 3 × 3 and 15 = 3 × 5 with the two 3s lit; the bubble is struck out

marks.m1: Keeko's bubble shows the row 9, 15 and the word stop
marks.m4: the bubble is struck out and the row 3, 5 appears

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks nine and fifteen share nothing, so the rows should stop after dividing by ten.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But nine is three times three, and fifteen is three times five.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Both have the prime three, so three goes into both numbers.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>We divide by three, and stop only at three and five, which share no prime.
